newsitem.title: UK: Blair's Labour defeats last left-wing challenge.
newsitem.headline: Blair's Labour defeats last left-wing challenge.

text.p: British opposition leader Tony Blair on Thursday brushed aside the last challenge to his authority from Labour's once-dominant left wing at his party's final conference before a general election.

A bid to force a future Labour government to guarantee pensions would be linked to earnings, championed by popular veteran and former cabinet minister Barbara Castle, was rejected by a margin of two to one by delegates.
The leadership, which has been at pains to avoid spelling out any tax or spending plans, argued such a pledge would commit the party to massive spending once in power.
Wednesday's debate was the first to pitch the left wing, increasingly marginalised by Blair since he took over in July 1994, against the modernising, centrist leadership.

But unlike previous Labour conferences, the debate, though passionate, was conducted in moderation, maintaining unity in a party famous in the 1980s for its bloody splits. The vote was taken on Wednesday but the result was delayed.

Blair, who electrified supporters and won over a sceptical press with his keynote speech on Tuesday, has warned that any spending commitments will be seized on by the Conservatives to portray Labour as an old-style tax and spend party.
Castle was appeased with a pledge that Labour would begin its review of welfare payments immediately rather than after an election due by May 1997.
This year's conference is the second in a row in which the party leadership has not been defeated on a key issue, underlining Blair's increasingly sure grip on the party.
Blair was set to crown the conference by receiving a ringing endorsement of his blueprint for the campaign expected to take him into office.

The conference was set later on Thursday to approve the campaign blueprint, "New Labour, new life for Britain" before it is sent to all party members for a mass ballot -- the first ever held in Britain -- on its contents.
Labour, out of power since 1979, has an opinion poll lead of more than 20 points over the Conservatives, who hold their annual conference next week.

But, despite the polls, senior figures are still worried Labour's lead could disappear and are haunted by their experience at the last election when the Conservatives came from behind to win their fourth successive election.

In a passionate appeal to party workers on Tuesday, deputy leader John Prescott said: "We don't want another day like Friday 10 April, 1992. The day we woke in horror to the prospect of five more years of Tory (Conservative) government."
But the Conservatives are reeling from a new sleaze scandal involving a former minister, which has reignited charges the government is out of touch and corrupted by too long in power.
Prime Minister John Major showed his anger by making it clear the former minister, Neil Hamilton, was not welcome at a reception on Tuesday at his official Downing Street residence.
The scandal involves payments to Hamilton by a political lobbyist. It hit the headlines again after Hamilton withdrew a libel action against the Guardian newspaper which broke the story.
Major also faces a weekend summit of European leaders in Dublin this weekend which could reignite the row in the Conservative party over a European single currency.
